title: Wellbeing Isn't Cake in the Staff Room. It's Professionalism Done Properly.
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes challenges the common equation of staff wellbeing with gestures of comfort like cake, beanbags and mindfulness sessions, arguing these do not touch the deeper sources of teacher exhaustion. Drawing on a meta-analysis of 17 studies on professional development and educator wellbeing, she argues that wellbeing grows from becoming more confident and competent at the work itself, not from taking a break from it. She links this to belonging: teachers who choose their own CPD report greater wellbeing than those whose participation is mandated, because agency signals institutional trust. The piece argues that mentoring, in particular, is an underrated wellbeing intervention because it replaces uncertainty with competence and confidence. Hughes concludes that schools have wrongly separated wellbeing initiatives from professional development, when genuine flourishing is the natural byproduct of feeling trusted, competent and connected to purpose.
points: Hughes reframes wellbeing not as comfort but as competence, arguing that professional development builds wellbeing by making teachers feel more capable, not merely less busy.
She uses the finding that voluntary CPD participation predicts greater wellbeing than mandated participation to argue that agency, not content, is what signals institutional trust.
Her claim that mentoring may be an underused wellbeing strategy links directly to her broader argument that competence-building, not reassurance, produces durable teacher confidence.
She criticises the structural separation of CPD and wellbeing teams in schools, arguing that any wellbeing strategy ignoring classroom realities will fail to have lasting impact.
quotes: The teacher who leaves school exhausted every evening doesn't suddenly become well because someone remembered to buy flapjacks. The ECT who is quietly wondering whether they belong in the profession isn't reassured by a fruit bowl.

Looking across 17 intervention studies, the researchers found that professional development had a positive impact on educators' wellbeing - not because it gave people a break from teaching, but because it helped them become more confident, more capable and more professionally fulfilled.

One of the strongest results showed that teachers who chose to participate in professional development experienced greater wellbeing than those whose participation was mandated. That isn't really about attendance. It's about agency.

This paper also made me wonder whether we have underestimated mentoring as a wellbeing intervention because excellent mentoring reduces uncertainty and builds competence. It replaces anxiety with clarity.

By all means, keep the cake. Just don't mistake it for the foundations. The foundations are much more substantial than that. They are built through excellent mentoring, thoughtful leadership, purposeful professional development and a culture that takes people's professional growth seriously.
